archetype.name: Dual-Threat (raw)
archetype.definition: A 6-foot-5, 236-pound third-year backup whose legs already produce value, while his pocket game (processing, rhythm throws, avoiding sacks) is unfinished.

report.headline: One start, seven sacks, real legs: a runner still learning to play quarterback
report.take:
Joe Milton III got his first start in Week 9 because Philadelphia had already cycled through Jalen Hurts and Tanner McKee. The 11-19 home loss to the Giants showed both sides of him. He went 18-of-34 for 169 yards with no touchdowns and no interceptions, took 7 sacks, and lost a fumble. He also led every qualifying quarterback in rushing yards per game with 64. His -13.5 passing EPA ranks 53rd of 54 for the week. Every number here is one game in one offense, missing DeVonta Smith and Dontayvion Wicks.

The sacks drove the result. His 17.1% sack rate is more than double the league's 7.9%, and 58.3% of his pressures became sacks, last among charted passers. That isn't simply a porous line. The offense ranks 22nd in hit rate allowed, which is middling, and he held the ball 3.12 seconds while throwing short of the sticks on average (-1.45 air yards to sticks). That pattern belongs to a quarterback who doesn't see the answer quickly and then tries to buy time. Sometimes the extra time paid off: 6 scrambles for 50 yards, at +0.392 EPA per scramble and 2 first downs. The scrambles did not come close to covering the sacks, though, and third down was the worst of it: -10.4 EPA on 11 plays, a 9.1% conversion rate, facing 8.1 yards to go on average.

The topline hides that the hardest throws were his best. On 9 attempts at 10-19 air yards he posted +0.355 EPA, a 66.7% success rate and +8.5 CPOE. The easy ones failed. Throws under 10 yards produced -0.239 EPA per play with a 15% success rate and -16.7 CPOE, and screens and flat throws behind the line were 0-for-6 on success. That is unusual, and it points to touch and timing on quick game rather than arm talent. The 0-for-4 deep line is too few throws to judge. The zero interceptions on 34 attempts look partly lucky given his 20.6% bad-throw rate, among the worst charted.

With one game and no career line to compare against, this is a scouting snapshot, not a verdict. The bye gave him two weeks of first-team reps. Smith and Wicks both carry Nov. 22 return estimates, which would put real receivers next to Makai Lemon and Dallas Goedert, the only two targets he was positive with. If the quick game gets cleaner with better spacing, the legs make for a floor. If the sack habit holds, he will keep killing drives.

strengths.title: Legs create real yards
strengths.body: He was the top qualifier in rushing yards per game in his only start, and most of it came from scrambles, which added value rather than just yardage. At his size, with a long-developing pocket, scrambling is going to stay in his game. It is the part of his profile most likely to carry over week to week.

strengths.title: Intermediate throws worked
strengths.body: The 10-19 yard window was the one area where he was efficient and accurate above expectation. Throws there reward his size and arm and depend less on quick-game timing. It is only 9 attempts, so treat it as a hint about where the offense should live, not a settled skill.

concerns.title: Pressure turns into sacks
concerns.body: A 58.3% pressure-to-sack rate paired with a 3.12-second time to throw is the profile of a passer who holds the ball rather than one whose line collapses. The scrambles show the upside of extending plays, but the sacks cost far more, especially on third down. This is the trait most likely to define his starts until he speeds up his reads, and it does not fix itself between games.

concerns.title: Quick game broke down
concerns.body: Throws under 10 air yards, normally the easiest completions, were his worst area by efficiency and accuracy. That suggests timing and ball placement problems on rhythm throws, which matches the 20.6% bad-throw rate. Some of it is a depleted receiver room. Most of it looks like the rawness you would expect from a sixth-round pick with little game experience.

concerns.title: Third downs became drive killers
concerns.body: Third down produced -10.4 EPA on 11 plays and one conversion. The Eagles left him in long yardage, and he answered with sacks and incompletions. Until early downs improve, this split will keep sinking his totals.

trend.note: One start, so there is no trajectory yet. The only baseline is a -13.5 EPA debut against a mid-pack Giants defense now ranked 14th.

nextGame.headline: Pittsburgh's pass rush tests his biggest flaw directly
nextGame.body:
Pittsburgh is an 11th-ranked defense by EPA with the 7th-best sack rate. That attacks his worst habit: holding the ball and absorbing sacks. Its run defense ranks 7th, which squeezes the designed-run part of his game, though scrambles come from broken pass plays rather than called runs. There are openings. The Steelers rank 23rd in deep EPA allowed and 25th in explosive pass rate allowed, they give quarterbacks the 27th-most yards per game, and tight ends have hit them hard. The Book has Philadelphia as a 4.5-point home underdog with a 38.5 total, which projects a low-scoring, grind-it-out game. The forecast is early but worth flagging: gusts near 29 mph and rain showers would hurt a passer who already struggles with timing.

Availability on his side matters most. DeVonta Smith (87% of snaps) and Dontayvion Wicks (80%) were both out with Nov. 22 return estimates. Getting either back would push Darius Cooper and his -0.383 EPA per target down the pecking order and give Milton a real outside option. Will Shipley's practice window has opened, which adds a pass-catching back if he is activated. On Pittsburgh's side, guard Mason McCormick is doubtful. Receivers Michael Pittman Jr. and Roman Wilson may return, which could give the Steelers enough offense against a 26th-ranked Eagles pass defense to push Philadelphia into a passing script Milton isn't built for.

keyMatchups.title: Steelers sack rate vs. his holds
keyMatchups.body: A top-10 sack defense against the quarterback with the worst pressure-to-sack rate among charted passers is the central question of the game. If he doesn't get the ball out faster after two weeks of reps, expect another multi-sack day and stalled third downs.

keyMatchups.title: Goedert against a weak spot
keyMatchups.body: Pittsburgh ranks 30th in EPA per play allowed to the top tight end, and Goedert was one of only two Eagles targets Milton was positive with. Tight-end throws in the intermediate range line up with the one window where Milton was efficient.

keyMatchups.title: WR1 coverage is stingy
keyMatchups.body: Pittsburgh ranks 3rd in EPA allowed to opposing No. 1 receivers. That dulls the Lemon connection, which was his best receiver pairing in Week 9, and makes Smith's return matter less as a matchup edge than as plain depth.

nextGame.watch: How quickly he gets the ball out on early downs. Fewer than four sacks would be the clearest sign the bye helped.

restOfSeason.body:
This projection rests on one game. The legs look sustainable: a quarterback this size who scrambles once every several dropbacks will keep producing rushing yards and fantasy floor. The zero interceptions do not look sustainable. A bad-throw rate above 20% usually catches up, so expect turnovers to arrive. The sack rate should come down from 17.1% simply because that number is extreme, but his tendency to hold the ball suggests it will stay well above league average. Projected range: roughly 150-205 passing yards, about half a touchdown to one-plus per game, 30-55 rushing yards, and 3-5 sacks a game.

The upside case needs Smith and Wicks back and an offense built around intermediate throws and designed movement. The downside case is that Hurts or McKee retakes the job if the sacks and third-down failures continue. The depth chart lists Milton as QB1 only as of Nov. 17, and the starts already show a team willing to rotate.
swingFactors: Whether he speeds up his reads after the bye
Job security behind Hurts and McKee

confidence.note: One start, no prior-season data, depleted receivers.
